provenance: legacy SemStreams capture; not a SemEngine result

constraints.rationale: The answer-path audit names the production synthesizer's missing-information instruction, temperature 0.3, 500-token limit, 15-second deadline and three retries as transport semantics every replay must preserve; the synthesis record reports the driver importing NewLLMAnswerSynthesizer with exactly those settings. Anyone judging whether the replay was faithful needs the audit's requirements next to the record's confirmation.

The guide defines the shared code precheck (filter passages by audience, allow when a required fact key has exactly one supplied value, defer when it is missing or conflicting). The source-pilot record reports that precheck resolving H01 and H02 before any model call and leaving 22 cases unresolved; the counts there are only readable against the rules here.

The laptop guide's compare:metal/compare:cpu description (same pinned Qwen3.5-4B GGUF and llama.cpp revision, JSON versus one-token scores, prefix reuse disabled, 96 measured calls per format) is the run whose exact conditions the scoring record's Metal section documents, and the guide points to that record for method and evidence. Changing the comparison task means changing both.

The smaller-Qwen record reuses the specialist evaluation's 120-query cohort, nine operations and literal binder, and its 'historical improved rules 95' and 'historical Qwen3.5-4B 111' rows are frozen references copied from the specialist held-out table rather than reruns. The 2B/1.7B gates are measured against that table, so the two records carry one comparison.

The history table lists the arms (actual keyword rules, rules plus BM25 at 0.7 and at 0.9, Qwen JSON, Kev) and their 23/32 and invalid-tuple counts; the validation record's contract defines those arms (BM25 only after the keyword tier yields no hints, Kev answering three native Choice questions) and the grading rule that a correct operation with a wrong argument is wrong. The numbers in one are uninterpretable without the contract in the other.

Both record the 2026-10-09 llama.cpp Metal throughput outcome: prompt processing at about 440 to 570 tokens per second regardless of slot count, Kev's only gain being 2.35x head grouping, still slower than Qwen JSON. The research document explains why Kev gained nothing from slots (embedding mode, one slot's prompt per compute step) and names the pre-declared readings that the history's cell table resolves.

The investigation's closeout status summarises the SGLang/MLX probe (failed warmup, then schema JSON, scores and decision bundles passing after --disable-radix-cache, bounded but not graceful shutdown, compatibility rather than performance). The scoring record's compatibility section holds the detail those sentences rest on: eight HTTP calls on one fixture, the cached path untested, the -9 exit analysis.

The Decision commits to packaging llama.cpp's native /v1/systemone with pinned Kev-4B Q4_K_M and keeping service code to bounds, health and forwarding; the bootstrap record is the local validation of that packaging (final CPU image loads the pinned model, serves native Choice/Score/Noul, passes contract checks, favours Kev at substantial CPU cost). The research document explicitly separates its source review from this validation record, so the two are meant to be read as decision and outcome.

The guide's statement that semsource's historical fusion scorecard passed all seven loose-language queries and so shows no demonstrated need for an added classifier is a summary of the audit's scorecard table and its 'left the proposed embedding-classifier tier unfed' finding, and the guide defers to the audit for that evidence. One is the claim, the other the data and caveats behind it.

The selection review records the owner approving Julia as the single challenger and summarises its CPU diagnostic (159 ms median, 24/48 correct, excessive deferral) as supporting the cost hypothesis but not routing quality; the history entry is the full diagnostic result (39 unknown selections, 23 unnecessary fallbacks, 530 MiB peak) that the selection consequence rests on.

Both are the same-shaped abstention table (thresholds 0.5/0.7/0.9, accepted over total, errors among accepted, 'not calibrated'). The first thresholds Kev's native SystemOne Choice probabilities through the semselect guard on the CPU bootstrap; the second thresholds ordinary Qwen's normalised first-token logprobs from the evaluation-only scorer that bypasses the guard. Different model, different score semantics, different experiment; the laptop guide says the scorer is evaluation code while the service serves Kev's native readouts.

Same M3 Pro, same llama.cpp pin, same 24-case routing smoke, same date, same Qwen3.5-4B Q4_K_M, same row names (valid, correct, order flips, p50, p95). But the Metal validation compares two models with prefix caching on, while the scoring table compares two output formats of one model with caching off; the laptop guide states the scoring latencies are not interchangeable with the cache-enabled model comparison. Grouping them invites reading Qwen 288 ms against Qwen 673 ms as one measurement.

Both are 'Reproduction and checks' closers with the same harness boilerplate: task check passed Go race tests, formatting, vet and Compose validation; Python ran N tests with one process-group timeout test skipped for EPERM. One reproduces the Qwen output-format scoring comparison (task compare:metal/cpu), the other the answerability teaching run (task answerability:metal); the shared sentences are about the repository's test harness, not either experiment.

Both lean on the word 'gate': 'Frozen gate | Required | Observed' and 'failed seven prerequisite gates' in one, '88 gate deferrals', 'both gates allowed only S09' and 'strict gate labels' in the other. In the specialist record a gate is a frozen acceptance criterion for promoting a classifier; in the synthesis record a gate is a model's allow/defer decision placed in front of the answer generator. Same term, unrelated responsibilities.

Both describe a decision API in the same vocabulary: System One shape, option probabilities normalised over candidates, 'not calibrated correctness'. The semstreams chunk specifies the pinned llama.cpp /v1/systemone Choice/Score/Noul fields that semselect's packaging and any adapter must preserve; the SGLang chunk describes SGLang's /v1/decisions token-score mechanism for the isolated investigation, which the investigation itself says shares API shape but not training, calibration or accuracy.

Both read as 'Kev native SystemOne versus Qwen schema-constrained JSON on Metal, normal and reversed candidate order, no prompt tuning'. The Metal method is the 24-case ticket-routing smoke with one four-way Choice; the query-routing contract is the SemStreams classifier-hint task with three Choice heads (operation, node, field) and tuple grading, which the results history calls a separate task. The shared method boilerplate hides different workloads and metrics.

Both are shell reproduction blocks of python3 script invocations with --output results/... paths and task commands, the kind of generic scaffold that clusters on shape alone. One drives the CPU bootstrap routing smoke (scripts/measure.py wrapping scripts/evaluate.py against semselect and seminstruct); the other drives the query-routing experiment's runner.py stages and report.py. Nothing but the command-block form is shared.

Both talk about communities, frozen fixtures, review and defer over a SemSource graph. The answer-path chunk freezes query-time CommunitySummary objects as inputs to the answer generator for the synthesis replay; the SemEngine chunk proposes a reviewer over semantic virtual-edge candidates before communities are recomputed, a graph-refinement workload the guide says the answer-path audit does not inform.

The same artifact appears in both: the seminstruct container with llama.cpp b8994 and Qwen3-0.6B Q4_K_M, four slots, the pinned ARM64 image. In the research document it is the label-only routing comparator and the basis of a service-economics argument about consolidating semselect into seminstruct; in the synthesis record it is the shipped Tier 2 answer generator whose unsupported assertions the gates are measured against. Shared pins, unrelated roles.

Both are NVIDIA/CUDA follow-up plans listing what to record (driver, CUDA toolchain, GPU and VRAM, model hashes, launch flags) before claiming support. The laptop chunk plans a CUDA build of the pinned llama.cpp launcher to rerun the same primitives and 48-request routing evaluation; the SGLang chunk plans an SGLang serving comparison on a 3090 or DGX Spark for the direct-scoring question, and the project keeps SGLang results separate from llama.cpp results by rule.
